title: AI Food and Drink Product Videos | AIVideosUGC
description: Make AI food and drink product videos: slow pours, plated serving shots, and packaging scenes from one photo of your can, bag, or jar. Upload yours and try it.
h1: AI Food and Drink Product Videos: Pours, Plates, and Packaging
lead: AI food and drink product videos show the fizz, the crumb, and the pack on the shelf. Start with a photo of your can, bottle, bag, or jar, then describe the moment you want people to see.
card: Pours, plates and packs on the shelf, in photos and short clips.
intro: Show the package clearly, then use a serving scene to show the product’s color, texture, or portion. A cold brew needs beads of condensation on the glass, a hot sauce needs a drizzle over tacos, and granola can be shown with a bowl of milk and berries. Packaging matters just as much, because that is what shoppers look for on a store shelf and in a delivery app.

Send in a clean shot of the package and spell out the serving moment: a can cracking open over ice, a cookie snapping in half, honey dripping from a dipper onto toast. Six- or ten-second vertical clips suit TikTok and Reels, while square photos fit your store and marketplace listings. Prices and offers are easiest to get right when you type them in afterward with Canva or CapCut.

ideas.d: Show your pasta sauce on a bowl of rigatoni or your spice blend on roasted vegetables, so shoppers see the finished dish and not just the jar.
Place a bag of coffee beans on a kitchen shelf, a snack box in a lunch bag, or a bottle of olive oil beside a cutting board. Upload a photo with the label sharp and facing forward.
A limited flavor or a holiday tin gets a short clip and a square still for your announcement post. Add the release date and price yourself so they appear exactly as intended.

faq.q: Will my ingredient list and nutrition facts look right in the image?
faq.a: Don't rely on the image for that. Small print on packaging may not come out exactly as printed, and ingredients, allergens, and nutrition facts should always match your real package. If buyers need to see them, use a clear photo of the actual label.

faq.q: Can I show a drink being poured if I only have a photo of the can?
faq.a: Yes. Describe the glass, the ice, and the color of the liquid, like "amber iced tea poured over ice in a tall glass." The more precise you are about color and texture, the closer the pour looks to your real drink.

faq.q: How long should a food video be for TikTok?
faq.a: Short is usually enough: 6 or 10 seconds covers a single moment like a pour or a first bite. Choose 15 seconds when you want two moments, such as the pack opening and then the plated food.

faq.q: Should I spray water on my can for a cold, fresh look?
faq.a: No need. Ask for condensation in your description instead, then wipe off fingerprints and photograph the dry can near a window with the light coming from the side.

overview.h2: Make the serving moment easy to picture

items.d: A clear front-facing can, bag, bottle, or jar anchors the scene. Add a separate source for the back or side when the package information matters, because small generated lettering is not a substitute for the real label.
A pour, crack, drizzle, snap, scoop, or plated finish is enough for a useful short clip. Keep ingredients, allergens, nutrition, and price on the verified package photo or product listing.

input_guide.h2: Prepare a food or drink upload

items.d: Photograph the can, bottle, pouch, box, or jar upright with the front label visible. Include the cap, lid, and base if they define the product.
Add a separate reference for crumb, sauce thickness, coffee color, fizz, tea leaves, or a cut surface when that detail carries the appeal.
Remove fingerprints and use side light for glossy cans and bottles. Ask for condensation or steam in the description rather than spraying the source.
For a multipack, gift box, or variety set, arrange every flavor or item in one frame so shoppers can count what arrives.
Name the glass, plate, table, lunch bag, shelf, or cutting board and keep the action focused on the food rather than invented label text.

scene_recipes.h2: Food and drink scenes you can describe

items.d: A chilled coffee bottle pouring over ice into a tall clear glass on a kitchen counter, condensation on the bottle, front label facing camera.
A hot-sauce bottle beside tacos while a glossy red drizzle crosses the top, close crop on the bottle cap and serving texture.
A granola cluster breaking over a bowl of yogurt and berries, the jar behind it on a linen breakfast table.
A tea pouch standing on a pantry shelf beside a mug and a small scoop, with the pouch front fully readable from a distance.

results.h2: What the food set can deliver

items.d: A pour, plate, drizzle, or break shows how the product might appear in a meal or routine.
Use square product stills and a clean shelf scene to keep the actual pack central in a gallery.
Use 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9 as the main choices, with 4:3 and 3:4 available for other crops; choose 6, 10, or 15 seconds for the action.
The tool shows the credit cost before you start, so you can choose a photo or clip that fits the product story.
The [FAQ](/faq) covers commercial-use details and whether downloads include a watermark.
Compare flavor, size, ingredient panel, nutrition values, allergen callouts, and count with the real product.
Place price, discount, launch date, stock note, and serving instructions in an approved layout where every character is controlled.
AIVideosUGC does not add voiceover, music, or captions; add verified ingredients and nutrition details, then caption the serving action in your editor.

good.d: Coffee, tea, snacks, sauces, condiments, jars, pouches, cans, and boxed sets with a visible package.
Products that can be poured, drizzled, scooped, plated, opened, or broken in one clear moment.
New flavors, lunch moments, pantry shelves, gifting, and seasonal serving scenes.

not_ideal.d: Use a real package photo for ingredients, allergens, nutrition, and required notices.
